desc:
The array nums contains distinct integers. In one move you may swap the elements at any two positions. Return the minimum number of moves needed to arrange nums in ascending order.

Example: nums = [4, 3, 1, 2] returns 3: swap positions 0 and 2 to get [1, 3, 4, 2], positions 1 and 3 to get [1, 2, 4, 3], and positions 2 and 3 to finish. Two swaps are not enough.
hints: Replace each value by its rank (its position in the sorted order). Now the array is a permutation of 0..n-1 and the target is the identity.
Draw an arrow from position i to the position where nums[i] should go. These arrows split the positions into cycles. A cycle of length 1 is already in place.
A cycle of length L can be fixed with L - 1 swaps and not with fewer. So the answer is n minus the number of cycles.
editorial: Sort the indices by value to find the target position of each element. The map i -> target(i) is a permutation, so it breaks into disjoint cycles. Every swap changes the number of cycles by exactly one (it either merges two cycles or splits one), and the sorted arrangement has n cycles (all of length 1), so at least n - cycles swaps are needed. Conversely, a cycle of length L is resolved by L - 1 swaps that each put one element into its final position, so the bound is achieved.
The work is a sort, O(n log n), followed by an O(n) cycle count. Because the values are distinct there is no ambiguity in the target positions; with duplicates the problem would be much harder.
solution:
def minSwapsToSort(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: nums[i])
    seen = [False] * n
    swaps = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if not seen[i]:
            length = 0
            j = i
            while not seen[j]:
                seen[j] = True
                j = order[j]
                length += 1
            swaps += length - 1
    return swaps
